details:
**Ark and the Great Flood**
God told Noah to build an ark of gopher wood, 300 cubits long, 50 wide, and 30 high, to save his family and the animals from a flood that would destroy the corrupt world. Rain fell for forty days and forty nights; Noah brought two of every kind of animal aboard, and seven pairs of each clean animal.

**Rainbow Covenant**
After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and all living things, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood, and set a rainbow in the clouds as its sign. God also says, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man."

**Shem, Ham, and Japheth**
Noah's three sons, who survived the flood with their wives and are traditionally seen as the ancestors of all later peoples: Shem of the Semites, Ham of peoples of Africa and Canaan, and Japheth of peoples to the north and west.

**Curse of Ham (Curse of Canaan)**
After the flood, Noah planted a vineyard, got drunk, and lay naked in his tent. Ham saw his father's "nakedness" and told his brothers, who covered Noah while looking away; when Noah awoke he cursed Ham's son Canaan to be "the lowest of slaves" to his brothers. This passage was later misused to justify the enslavement of Black Africans.

**Dove with an olive leaf**
To learn whether the waters had receded, Noah first sent out a raven, which flew back and forth, and then a dove. The dove returned the first time, came back with a freshly plucked olive leaf the second time, and did not return the third time, showing that dry land had appeared.

**First vineyard and first wine**
Noah is described as a man of the soil who planted the first vineyard, and tradition makes him the first person to make and drink wine. His drunkenness sets up the Curse of Ham episode.

**Mount Ararat**
The "mountains of Ararat," where the ark came to rest in the Genesis account. The name is now attached to the peak in eastern Turkey.

**Nuh and Mount Judi**
In Islam, Noah is the prophet Nuh, generally listed third among the 25 prophets named in the Quran, after Adam and Idris. In the Quran (Surah Hud) the ark comes to rest on Mount Judi rather than Ararat.

**Surah Nuh (Sura 71)**
The 71st chapter of the Quran, named for Noah. It describes his long, unsuccessful preaching to his people and his reminder that God made the moon a light and the sun a lamp, and it ends with his prayer that the unbelievers be destroyed.

**Noah's unbelieving son (Yam or Canaan)**
In Islamic tradition, one of Noah's sons, often named Yam or Kan'an, refused to board the ark and said he would climb a mountain to escape the waters. He drowned in the flood.

**Table of Nations**
Genesis 10, which lists the descendants of Shem, Ham, and Japheth by lineage and geography. Its roughly seventy names are traditionally read as the "seventy nations" of the world.

**Noahide Laws**
In Jewish tradition, seven commandments given to Noah that bind all humanity, not just Jews. They include bans on idolatry, blasphemy, murder, sexual immorality, theft, and eating flesh torn from a living animal, plus a requirement to set up courts of justice.

**"Blameless in his generation" and "walked with God"**
Genesis 6:9 describes Noah as a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, who walked with God. This is why he alone found favor when God decided to destroy the world.

**Son of Lamech**
Noah's father was Lamech, a descendant of Seth, and his grandfather was Methuselah. Lamech named him Noah, saying he would bring relief from the toil of working the cursed ground.

**Noah as the archangel Gabriel**
In the theology of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), Joseph Smith taught that Noah is the same being as the archangel Gabriel, who appeared in mortal form as Noah.
